THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: We will begin, today, with an overview of joints and joint classifications, and then we will move on to more detailed discussion of fibrous joints, cartilaginous joints, and finally synovial joints. We will finish up with an examination of body movement classifications.

slides.title: Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints
slides.body:
Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Let’s begin with Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints.

slides.title: Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints
slides.body:
Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints

Joint (articulation) - location where bones, or bone and cartilage, meet
movement – stability trade-off based on composition of joint

Stability

Movement

Stable joints: Suture joints of the skull.

Spinal movements. Credit: Cervical_Xray_Extension.jpg: Stillwaterisingderivative work: F. Lamiot, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Movable joints: Elbow and shoulder joints. Credit: Niwadare, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Joints, or articulations, are the location where bones, or bone and cartilage, come together.

While some joints allow for movement between the bones, others provide for stability and little or no movement. It is important to note that there is a traded-off between stability and movement, so joints cannot have both high stability and high movement. Thus, stable joints allow for little or no mobility between the adjacent bones. Conversely, joints that provide the most movement between bones are the least stable.

slides.title: Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints
slides.body:
Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints

Articulating surfaces:
fibrous connective tissue – little or no movement
e.g., skull sutures, joints holding tibia and fibia together
cartilage – little or no movement
e.g. vertebral column
lubricating fluid – wide range of movement
most bones in appendicular skeleton

Fibia and tibia. Credit: Hariadhi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Vertebrae. Credit: Stillwaterising, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Thumb joints. Credit: LittleT889, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The articulating surfaces of bones at stable types of joints, with little or no mobility, are strongly united to each other. For example, most of the joints of the skull are held together by fibrous connective tissue and do not allow for movement between the adjacent bones. This lack of mobility is important, because the skull bones serve to protect the brain. Similarly, other joints united by fibrous connective tissue allow for very little movement, which provides stability and weight-bearing support for the body. For example, the tibia and fibula of the leg are tightly united to give stability to the body when standing. 

At other joints, the bones are held together by cartilage, which permits limited movements between the bones. Thus, the joints of the vertebral column only allow for small movements between adjacent vertebrae, but when added together, these movements provide the flexibility that allows your body to twist, or bend to the front, back, or side. 

In contrast, at joints that allow for wide ranges of motion, the articulating surfaces of the bones are not directly united to each other. Instead, these surfaces are enclosed within a space filled with lubricating fluid, which allows the bones to move smoothly against each other. These joints provide greater mobility, but since the bones are free to move in relation to each other, the joint is less stable. Most of the joints between the bones of the appendicular skeleton are this freely moveable type of joint. These joints allow the muscles of the body to pull on a bone and thereby produce movement of that body region. Your ability to kick a soccer ball or pick up a fork depend on mobility at these types of joints.

slides.title: Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints
slides.body:
Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints

Classifications:
Structural
fibrous – fibrous connective tissue
cartilaginous – hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage
synovial - joint cavity filled with lubricating liquid
Functional - (arthroun = “to fasten by a joint”)
synarthrosis – immobile – some fibrous and cartilaginous joints
amphiarthrosis – slightly mobile – some fibrous and cartilaginous joints
diarthrosis – freely moveable – all synovial joints

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Joints can thus be classified both structurally and functionally. 

Structural classifications of joints take into account whether the adjacent bones are strongly anchored to each other by fibrous connective tissue or cartilage, or whether the adjacent bones articulate with each other within a fluid-filled space called a joint cavity. These differences serve to divide the joints of the body into three structural classifications. A fibrous joint is where the adjacent bones are united by fibrous connective tissue. At a cartilaginous joint, the bones are joined by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage. At a synovial joint, the articulating surfaces of the bones are not directly connected, but instead come into contact with each other within a joint cavity that is filled with a lubricating fluid. Synovial joints allow for free movement between the bones and are the most common joints of the body. These structural classifications will be discussed in parts 2-4 of this unit. But first, we also need to discuss functional classifications of joints.

Functional classifications describe the degree of movement available between the bones, ranging from immobile, to slightly mobile, to freely moveable joints. Joints are thus functionally classified as a synarthrosis or immobile joint, an amphiarthrosis or slightly moveable joint, or as a diarthrosis, or freely moveable joint. Note that arthroun means = “to fasten by a joint”. 

Depending on their location, fibrous joints may be functionally classified as a synarthrosis (immobile joint) or an amphiarthrosis (slightly mobile joint). 

Likewise, cartilaginous joints are also functionally classified as either a synarthrosis or an amphiarthrosis joint. 

All synovial joints, however, are functionally classified as a diarthrosis joint.

slides.title: Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints
slides.body:
Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints

Classifications:
synarthrosis
e.g., fibrous sutures between bones of the skull
function: protection

Suture Joints of Skull. The suture joints of the skull are an example of a synarthrosis, an immobile or essentially immobile joint.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: As stated, synarthrosis joints are immobile or nearly immobile joints. The immobile nature of these joints provides for a strong union between the articulating bones. This is important at locations where the bones provide protection for internal organs. Examples include the sutures, the fibrous joints between the bones of the skull that surround and protect the brain

slides.title: Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints
slides.body:
Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints

Classifications:
amphiarthrosis
e.g., fibrocartilage of intervertebral disk
function: support
function: limited movement
summed across all vertebrae, provides large range of movement

Intervertebral Disc. An intervertebral disc unites the bodies of adjacent vertebrae within the vertebral column. Each disc allows for limited movement between the vertebrae and thus functionally forms an amphiarthrosis type of joint. Intervertebral discs are made of fibrocartilage and thereby structurally form a symphysis type of cartilaginous joint.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: And as we also stated a couple of slides ago, an amphiarthrosis is a joint that has limited mobility. An example of this type of joint is the cartilaginous joint that unites the bodies of adjacent vertebrae. Filling the gap between the vertebrae is a thick pad of fibrocartilage called an intervertebral disc. Each intervertebral disc strongly unites the vertebrae but still allows for a limited amount of movement between them. However, the small movements available between adjacent vertebrae can sum together along the length of the vertebral column to provide for large ranges of body movements.

slides.title: Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints
slides.body:
Part 1: Overview and Classification of Joints

Classifications:
diarthrosis
e.g., all synovial joints 
function: movement
subcategories:
uniaxial 
movement in one plane
e.g., elbow joint
bend
biaxial
movement in two planes
e.g., metacarpophalangeal joint (knuckle joint) 
bend & spread
multiaxial (or polyaxial or triaxial)
e.g., shoulder joint; hip joint
bend anterior-posterior, bend medial-lateral, rotate along long axis

Elbow – uniaxial joint; Knuckles – biaxial joints. Credit: Niwadare, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Multiaxial Joint. A multiaxial joint, such as the hip joint, allows for three types of movement: anterior-posterior, medial-lateral, and rotational.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
And finally, we also mentioned that a diarthrosis is a freely mobile joint. These types of joints include all synovial joints of the body, which provide the majority of body movements. Most diarthrotic joints are found in the appendicular skeleton and thus give the limbs a wide range of motion.

These joints are divided into three categories, based on the number of axes of motion provided by each. An axis in anatomy is described as the movements in reference to the three anatomical planes: transverse, frontal, and sagittal. Thus, diarthroses are classified as uniaxial (for movement in one plane), biaxial (for movement in two planes), or multiaxial joints (for movement in all three anatomical planes).

A uniaxial joint only allows for a motion in a single plane (around a single axis). The elbow joint, which only allows for bending or straightening, is an example of a uniaxial joint. 

A biaxial joint allows for motions within two planes. An example of a biaxial joint is a metacarpophalangeal joint (or knuckle joint) of the hand. The joint allows for movement along one axis to produce bending or straightening of the finger, and movement along a second axis, which allows for spreading of the fingers away from each other and bringing them back together again. 

A joint that allows for several directions of movement is called a multiaxial joint (or polyaxial or triaxial, as well). This type of multiaxial diarthrotic joint allows for movement along three axes. The shoulder and hip joints are multiaxial joints. They allow the upper or lower limb to move in an anterior-posterior direction and a medial-lateral direction. In addition, the limb can also be rotated around its long axis. This third movement results in rotation of the limb so that its anterior surface is moved either toward or away from the midline of the body.

slides.title: Part 2: Fibrous Joints
slides.body:
Part 2: Fibrous Joints

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Let’s now move on to our first structural joints category within Part 2: Fibrous Joints.

slides.title: Part 2: Fibrous Joints
slides.body:
Part 2: Fibrous Joints

Fibrous joints
fibrous connective tissue connects bones; thus, no joint cavity
3 types:
suture - narrow fibrous joint between most bones of the skull
syndesmosis joint – holds parallel bones together
gomphosis - narrow fibrous joint between roots of tooth and bony socket in jaw

Fibrous Joints. Fibrous joints form strong connections between bones. (a) Sutures join most bones of the skull. (b) An interosseous membrane forms a syndesmosis between the radius and ulna bones of the forearm. (c) A gomphosis is a specialized fibrous joint that anchors a tooth to its socket in the jaw.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
At a fibrous joint, the adjacent bones are directly connected to each other by fibrous connective tissue, and thus the bones do not have a joint cavity between them. The gap between the bones may be narrow or wide. There are three types of fibrous joints. 

A suture is the narrow fibrous joint found between most bones of the skull. 

A syndesmosis joint holds parallel bones, like those in the arm and leg, together. 

A gomphosis is the narrow fibrous joint between the roots of a tooth and its bony socket in the jaw.

Let’s look at these in a little more detail

slides.title: Part 2: Fibrous Joints
slides.body:
Part 2: Fibrous Joints

Suture (“to bind or sew”) 
connects all skull bones except mandible
tight union that prevents most movement between the bones 
thus, classified as synarthrosis, although some sutures may allow for slight movements 
some sutures will ossify and be converted to bone (ossify)
e.g., baby to toddler

Fibrous Joints. Fibrous joints form strong connections between bones. (a) Sutures join most bones of the skull.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
All the bones of the skull, except for the mandible, are joined to each other by a fibrous joint called a suture. The fibrous connective tissue found at a suture (meaning “to bind or sew”) strongly unites the adjacent skull bones and thus helps to protect the brain and form the face. In adults, the skull bones are closely opposed, and fibrous connective tissue fills the narrow gap between the bones. The suture is frequently convoluted, forming a tight union that prevents most movement between the bones. Thus, skull sutures are functionally classified as a synarthrosis, although some sutures may allow for slight movements between the cranial bones.

At some sutures, the connective tissues will ossify and be converted into bone, causing the adjacent bones to fuse to each other. Examples of fusions between cranial bones are found both early and late in life.

slides.title: Part 2: Fibrous Joints
slides.body:
Part 2: Fibrous Joints

Syndesmosis (“fastened with a band”)
two parallel bones are united to each other by fibrous connective tissue
at wide gap between bones, forms interosseous membrane
at narrow gap between bones, forms ligaments
classified as an amphiarthrosis
although bones held parallel, some movement is possible
more between radius and ulna, so radius can rotate
less between tibia and fibula, to provide more strength and stability

Fibrous Joints. Fibrous joints form strong connections between bones (b) An interosseous membrane forms a syndesmosis between the radius and ulna bones of the forearm.

Tarsus (tarsal bones). Credit: BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A syndesmosis (meaning “fastened with a band”) is a type of fibrous joint in which two parallel bones are united to each other by fibrous connective tissue. The gap between the bones may be narrow, with the bones joined by ligaments, or the gap may be wide and filled in by a broad sheet of connective tissue called an interosseous membrane.

For example, in the forearm, the wide gap between the shaft portions of the radius and ulna bones are strongly united by an interosseous membrane. Similarly, in the leg, the shafts of the tibia and fibula are also united by an interosseous membrane. In addition, at the distal tibiofibular joint, the articulating surfaces of the bones lack cartilage and the narrow gap between the bones is anchored by fibrous connective tissue and ligaments. Together, the interosseous membrane and these ligaments form the tibiofibular syndesmosis.

The syndesmoses found in the forearm and leg serve to unite parallel bones and prevent their separation. However, a syndesmosis does not prevent all movement between the bones, and thus this type of fibrous joint is functionally classified as an amphiarthrosis. In the leg, the syndesmosis between the tibia and fibula strongly unites the bones, allows for little movement, and firmly locks the talus bone in place between the tibia and fibula at the ankle joint. This provides strength and stability to the leg and ankle, which are important during weight bearing. In the forearm, the interosseous membrane is flexible enough to allow for rotation of the radius bone during forearm movements. Thus, in contrast to the stability provided by the tibiofibular syndesmosis, the flexibility of the antebrachial interosseous membrane allows for the much greater mobility of the forearm.

slides.title: Part 2: Fibrous Joints
slides.body:
Part 2: Fibrous Joints

Gomphosis (“fastened with bolts”)
specialized fibrous joint that anchors the root of a tooth into its bony socket
also known as a peg-and-socket joint
numerous short bands of dense connective tissue, each of which is called a periodontal ligament
classified as a synarthrosis due to immobility

Fibrous Joints. Fibrous joints form strong connections between bones. (c) A gomphosis is a specialized fibrous joint that anchors a tooth to its socket in the jaw.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: A gomphosis (meaning “fastened with bolts”) is the specialized fibrous joint that anchors the root of a tooth into its bony socket within the maxillary bone (upper jaw) or mandible bone (lower jaw) of the skull. A gomphosis is also known as a peg-and-socket joint. Spanning between the bony walls of the socket and the root of the tooth are numerous short bands of dense connective tissue, each of which is called a periodontal ligament. Due to the immobility of a gomphosis, this type of joint is functionally classified as a synarthrosis.

slides.notes: Okay, now on to Part 3: Cartilaginous Joints.

slides.title: Part 3: Cartilaginous Joints
slides.body:
Part 3: Cartilaginous Joints

Cartilaginous joints
bones united by cartilage
tough but flexible
lack joint cavity
2 types:
synchondrosis – cartilaginous joint where bones are joined by hyaline cartilage (or bone united to cartilage like in rib cage) 
symphysis – where bones are joined by fibrocartilage

Cartilaginous Joints. At cartilaginous joints, bones are united by hyaline cartilage to form a synchondrosis or by fibrocartilage to form a symphysis. (a) The hyaline cartilage of the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) forms a synchondrosis that unites the shaft (diaphysis) and end (epiphysis) of a long bone and allows the bone to grow in length. (b) The pubic portions of the right and left hip bones of the pelvis are joined together by fibrocartilage, forming the pubic symphysis.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As the name indicates, at a cartilaginous joint, the adjacent bones are united by cartilage, a tough but flexible type of connective tissue.

These types of joints lack a joint cavity and involve bones that are joined together by either hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage. There are two types of cartilaginous joints:

A synchondrosis is a cartilaginous joint where the bones are joined by hyaline cartilage. Also classified as a synchondrosis are places where bone is united to a cartilage structure, such as between the anterior end of a rib and the costal cartilage of the thoracic cage. 

The second type of cartilaginous joint is a symphysis, where the bones are joined by fibrocartilage.

Let’s look at these in a little more detail

slides.title: Part 3: Cartilaginous Joints
slides.body:
Part 3: Cartilaginous Joints

Cartilaginous Joints. At cartilaginous joints, bones are united by hyaline cartilage to form a synchondrosis or by fibrocartilage to form a symphysis. (a) The hyaline cartilage of the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) forms a synchondrosis that unites the shaft (diaphysis) and end (epiphysis) of a long bone and allows the bone to grow in length.

Synchondrosis (“joined by cartilage”) 
bones are joined together by hyaline cartilage
or bone is united to hyaline cartilage
classified as synarthrosis, due to lack of movement
synchondrosis can be temporary
e.g., epiphyseal plate until long bone growth stops
e.g., fusion of ilium, ischium, and pubic portions of hip bone in childhood
synchondrosis can be permanent
e.g., some ribs in thoracic cage where anterior end is joined to costal cartilage

Pelvis. Adapted from: BruceBlaus. Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Costal cartilage. Adapted from:Anatomography, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A synchondrosis (meaning “joined by cartilage”) is a cartilaginous joint where bones are joined together by hyaline cartilage, or where bone is united to hyaline cartilage. A synchondrosis may be temporary or permanent. A temporary synchondrosis is the epiphyseal plate (growth plate) of a growing long bone. The epiphyseal plate is the region of growing hyaline cartilage that unites the diaphysis (shaft) of the bone to the epiphysis (end of the bone). But during the late teens and early 20s, growth of the cartilage slows and eventually stops when the epiphyseal plate is completely replaced by bone, fusing the diaphysis and epiphysis into a single adult bone. 

Growing layers of cartilage also form synchondroses that join together the ilium, ischium, and pubic portions of the hip bone during childhood and adolescence. When body growth stops, the cartilage disappears and is replaced by bone, forming synostoses and fusing the bony components together into the single hip bone of the adult. Similarly, the sacral vertebrae fuse together to form the adult sacrum.

Examples of permanent synchondroses are found in the thoracic cage, such as where the anterior end of most ribs is joined to its costal cartilage.

Due to the lack of movement between the bone and cartilage, both temporary and permanent synchondroses are functionally classified as a synarthrosis.

slides.title: Part 3: Cartilaginous Joints
slides.body:
Part 3: Cartilaginous Joints

Symphysis  (meaning “growing together”)
strong, but flexible
fibrocartilage (collagen fibres make it more resistant to pulling & bending than hyaline cartilage in synchondrosis)
classified as amphiarthrosis, due to limited movement
e.g., pubic symphysis (across narrow gap)
e.g., intervertebral symphysis (wide gap between bodies of adjacent vertebrae filled by fibrocartilage called intervertebral disc)

Cartilaginous Joints. At cartilaginous joints, bones are united by hyaline cartilage to form a synchondrosis or by fibrocartilage to form a symphysis. (b) The pubic portions of the right and left hip bones of the pelvis are joined together by fibrocartilage, forming the pubic symphysis.

Intervertebral Disc. An intervertebral disc unites the bodies of adjacent vertebrae within the vertebral column. Each disc allows for limited movement between the vertebrae and thus functionally forms an amphiarthrosis type of joint. Intervertebral discs are made of fibrocartilage and thereby structurally form a symphysis type of cartilaginous joint.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A cartilaginous joint where the bones are joined by fibrocartilage is called a symphysis (meaning “growing together”). Fibrocartilage is very strong because it contains numerous bundles of thick collagen fibers, thus giving it a much greater ability to resist pulling and bending forces when compared with hyaline cartilage. This gives symphyses the ability to strongly unite the adjacent bones but can still allow for limited movement to occur. Thus, a symphysis is functionally classified as an amphiarthrosis.

The gap separating the bones at a symphysis may be narrow or wide. An example in which the gap between the bones is narrow is the pubic symphysis, where the pubic portions of the right and left hip bones of the pelvis are joined together by fibrocartilage across a narrow gap.

The intervertebral symphysis is a wide symphysis located between the bodies of adjacent vertebrae of the vertebral column. Here a thick pad of fibrocartilage called an intervertebral disc strongly unites the adjacent vertebrae by filling the gap between them. The width of the intervertebral symphysis is important because it allows for small movements between the adjacent vertebrae. In addition, the thick intervertebral disc provides cushioning between the vertebrae, which is important when carrying heavy objects or during high-impact activities such as running or jumping.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Synovial joints
most common joint type
joint cavity present
fluid-filled space between articulating surfaces of bones
allows for increased mobility (vs. fibrous connective tissue or cartilage)
functionally classified as a diarthrosis

Synovial Joints. Synovial joints allow for smooth movements between the adjacent bones. The joint is surrounded by an articular capsule that defines a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid. The articulating surfaces of the bones are covered by a thin layer of articular cartilage. Ligaments support the joint by holding the bones together and resisting excess or abnormal joint motions.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the body. A key structural characteristic for a synovial joint that is not seen at fibrous or cartilaginous joints is the presence of a joint cavity. This fluid-filled space is the site at which the articulating surfaces of the bones contact each other. Also, unlike fibrous or cartilaginous joints, the articulating bone surfaces at a synovial joint are not directly connected to each other with fibrous connective tissue or cartilage. This gives the bones of a synovial joint the ability to move smoothly against each other, allowing for increased joint mobility.

The ability of the bones to move smoothly against each other within the joint cavity, and the freedom of joint movement this provides, means that each synovial joint is functionally classified as a diarthrosis.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Structural features of synovial joints:
articular capsule – (fibrous (a.k.a., dense) connective tissue) forms joint cavity walls
articular cartilage – hyaline cartilage layer protects articulating surfaces of bones
synovial membrane – lines inner surface of the articular capsule
membrane cells secrete lubricating synovial fluid (synovia = “a thick fluid”)
synovial fluid also provides nourishment to the articular cartilage (since cartilage does not contain blood vessels)

Synovial Joints. Synovial joints allow for smooth movements between the adjacent bones. The joint is surrounded by an articular capsule that defines a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid. The articulating surfaces of the bones are covered by a thin layer of articular cartilage. Ligaments support the joint by holding the bones together and resisting excess or abnormal joint motions.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The walls of the joint cavity are formed by the articular capsule, a fibrous connective tissue structure.

Friction between the bones at a synovial joint is prevented by the presence of the articular cartilage, a thin layer of hyaline cartilage that covers the entire articulating surface of each bone. However, unlike at a cartilaginous joint, the articular cartilages of each bone are not continuous with each other. Instead, the articular cartilage coating over the bone surface allows the articulating bones to move smoothly against each other without damaging the underlying bone tissue. 

Lining the inner surface of the articular capsule is a thin synovial membrane. The cells of this membrane secrete synovial fluid, a thick, slimy fluid that provides lubrication to further reduce friction between the bones of the joint. This fluid also provides nourishment to the articular cartilage, which does not contain blood vessels.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Structural features of synovial joints:
ligaments – (fibrous connective tissue) connect bones outside of articulating surfaces
limit range of motion, preventing excessive or abnormal joint movements
muscle tendons – (dense connective tissue) provide additional support
contraction of the muscles crossing a joint  allows muscle and its tendon to serve as an extra “dynamic ligament”

Bursae. Bursae are fluid-filled sacs that serve to prevent friction between skin, muscle, or tendon and an underlying bone. Three major bursae and a fat pad are part of the complex joint that unites the femur and tibia of the leg.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Outside of their articulating surfaces, the bones are connected together by ligaments, which are strong bands of fibrous connective tissue. These strengthen and support the joint by anchoring the bones together and preventing their separation. Ligaments allow for normal movements at a joint, but limit the range of these motions, thus preventing excessive or abnormal joint movements.

At many synovial joints, additional support is provided by the muscles and their tendons that act across the joint. A tendon is the dense connective tissue structure that attaches a muscle to bone. As forces acting on a joint increase, the body will automatically increase the overall strength of contraction of the muscles crossing that joint, thus allowing the muscle and its tendon to serve as a “dynamic ligament” to resist forces and support the joint. This type of indirect support by muscles is very important at the shoulder joint, for example, where the ligaments are relatively weak.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Articular disc at radius and ulna. Credit: Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Part 4: Synovial Joints

Additional synovial joint structures:
articular disc (or meniscus when large and C-shaped)
fibrocartilage structure present in some synovial joints
may act to strongly unite the bones of the joint to each other
e.g., at distal ends of the radius and ulna; sternoclavicular joints 
can provide shock absorption and cushioning 
e.g., knee meniscus
can serve to smooth the movements between the articulating bones
e.g., temporomandibular joint

https://www.gleneagles.com.sg/conditions-diseases/meniscus-tear/symptoms-causes

Knee meniscus. Credit: Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Articular disc at temporomandibular joint. Credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A few synovial joints of the body have a fibrocartilage structure located between the articulating bones. This is called an articular disc, which is generally small and oval-shaped, or a meniscus, which is larger and C-shaped. These structures can serve several functions, depending on the specific joint. 

In some places, an articular disc may act to strongly unite the bones of the joint to each other. Examples of this include the articular discs found at the sternoclavicular joint or between the distal ends of the radius and ulna bones. 

At other synovial joints, the disc can provide shock absorption and cushioning between the bones, which is the function of each meniscus within the knee joint. 

Finally, an articular disc can serve to smooth the movements between the articulating bones, as seen at the temporomandibular joint.

slides.body:

Additional synovial joint structures:
fat pad
serves as cushion between the bones

Bursae. Bursae are fluid-filled sacs that serve to prevent friction between skin, muscle, or tendon and an underlying bone. Three major bursae and a fat pad are part of the complex joint that unites the femur and tibia of the leg.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Some synovial joints also have a fat pad, which can serve as a cushion between the bones.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Additional synovial joint structures:
bursa
a thin connective tissue sac filled with lubricating liquid
separate adjacent structures to prevent friction

Bursae. Bursae are fluid-filled sacs that serve to prevent friction between skin, muscle, or tendon and an underlying bone. Three major bursae and a fat pad are part of the complex joint that unites the femur and tibia of the leg.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Additional structures located outside of a synovial joint serve to prevent friction between the bones of the joint and the overlying muscle tendons or skin. A bursa is a thin connective tissue sac filled with lubricating liquid. Bursae are located in regions where skin, ligaments, muscles, or muscle tendons can rub against each other, usually near a body joint. Bursae reduce friction by separating the adjacent structures, preventing them from rubbing directly against each other.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

6 types of synovial joints
pivot
hinge
condyloid
saddle
plane
ball-and socket

Types of Synovial Joints. The six types of synovial joints allow the body to move in a variety of ways. (a) Pivot joints allow for rotation around an axis, such as between the first and second cervical vertebrae, which allows for side-to-side rotation of the head. (b) The hinge joint of the elbow works like a door hinge. (c) The articulation between the trapezium carpal bone and the first metacarpal bone at the base of the thumb is a saddle joint. (d) Plane joints, such as those between the tarsal bones of the foot, allow for limited gliding movements between bones. (e) The radiocarpal joint of the wrist is a condyloid joint. (f) The hip and shoulder joints are the only ball-and-socket joints of the body.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Synovial joints are subdivided based on the shapes of the articulating surfaces of the bones that form each joint. 

The six types of synovial joints are pivot, hinge, condyloid, saddle, plane, and ball-and socket-joints.

Let’s look at these in more detail.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Types of Synovial Joints. The six types of synovial joints allow the body to move in a variety of ways. (a) Pivot joints allow for rotation around an axis, such as between the first and second cervical vertebrae, which allows for side-to-side rotation of the head

Part 4: Synovial Joints

Pivot joint
rounded portion of bone enclosed within a ring of another bone and ligament 
bone rotates within this ring
uniaxial – rotation is around a single axis
e.g., atlantoaxial joint, found between the C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) vertebrae
e.g., proximal radioulnar joint – head of radius encircled by ligament that holds it in place as it articulates ulna – rotation of the radius allows for forearm movements

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Elbow joint. Credit: AdamC30, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes:
Pivot Joints: At a pivot joint, a rounded portion of a bone is enclosed within a ring formed partially by the articulation with another bone and partially by a ligament. The bone rotates within this ring. Since the rotation is around a single axis, pivot joints are functionally classified as a uniaxial joint. 

An example of a pivot joint is the atlantoaxial joint, found between the C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) vertebrae. 

A second example of a pivot joint is found at the proximal radioulnar joint. Here, the head of the radius is largely encircled by a ligament that holds it in place as it articulates with the radial notch of the ulna. Rotation of the radius allows for forearm movements.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Pivot joint
forearm rotation allows for directional movements of the hands:
in the anatomical position, the hand is held supinated
when your arms are held outward, supination has the palms facing upward, as if to hold a bowl of soup
the reverse position is called pronation

Pronation and supination.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Arm rotation allows for directional movements of the hands. In the anatomical position, the hand is held supinated. When your arms are held outward, supination has the palms of your hands facing upward, as if to hold a bowl of soup. The reverse position is called pronation.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Types of Synovial Joints. The six types of synovial joints allow the body to move in a variety of ways. (b) The hinge joint of the elbow works like a door hinge.

Part 4: Synovial Joints

Hinge joint
convex end of one bone articulates with the concave end of the adjoining bone 
uniaxial – allows only for angular movements –  bending (flexion) and straightening (extension) motions along a single axis
e.g., elbow joint – articulation between the humerus and the ulna
e.g., knee, ankle, interphalangeal joints (between the phalanx bones of the fingers and toes)

Hinge joint. Adapted from: Produnis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Arm movements. Credit: Modified from Z-Anatomy (CC-BY-SA 4.0) by D. Rittenhouse.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Hinge Joint: In a hinge joint, the convex end of one bone articulates with the concave end of the adjoining bone. This type of joint allows only for angular movements – bending and straightening motions along a single axis – and thus hinge joints are functionally classified as uniaxial joints. 

A good example is the elbow joint, with the articulation between the humerus and the ulna. 

Other hinge joints of the body include the knee, ankle, and interphalangeal joints between the phalanx bones of the fingers and toes.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Types of Synovial Joints. The six types of synovial joints allow the body to move in a variety of ways. (e) The radiocarpal joint of the wrist is a condyloid joint.

Part 4: Synovial Joints

Condyloid joint (ellipsoid joint)
shallow depression at the end of one bone articulates with a rounded structure from an adjacent bone or bones
biaxial – allow for two planes of angular movement
e.g., knuckle (metacarpophalangeal) joints (between the distal end of a metacarpal bone and the proximal phalanx bone) 
bend fingers OR spread fingers
e.g., radiocarpal joint of the wrist
flexion or extension (toward anterior, while standing in anatomical position, as when forming fist, or posterior, as when flattening out your hand) OR adduction and abduction (toward medial or lateral)

Ellipsoid joint. Adapted from: Produnis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

(away from midline in anat. pos.)

(toward midline in anat. position)

Abduction

Adduction

Adduction and abduction of wrist. Adapted from: Yahia.Mokhtar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Condyloid Joint: At condyloid joints (also known as ellipsoid joints), the shallow depression at the end of one bone articulates with a rounded structure from an adjacent bone or bones. 

The knuckle (metacarpophalangeal) joints of the hand between the distal end of a metacarpal bone and the proximal phalanx bone are condyloid joints.

Another example is the radiocarpal joint of the wrist, between the shallow depression at the distal end of the radius bone and three of the carpal bones. 

Functionally, condyloid joints are biaxial joints that allow for two planes of angular movement. One movement involves the bending and straightening of the fingers or the anterior-posterior movements of the hand (the flexion or extension of the hand). The second movement is a side-to-side movement, which allows you to spread your fingers apart and bring them together, or to move your hand in a medial-going (adduction) or lateral-going (abduction) direction.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Types of Synovial Joints. The six types of synovial joints allow the body to move in a variety of ways. (c) The articulation between the trapezium carpal bone and the first metacarpal bone at the base of the thumb is a saddle joint.

Part 4: Synovial Joints

Saddle joint
both articulating bone surfaces have a saddle shape – concave in one direction and convex in the other
biaxial – allow for two planes of angular movement
e.g., first carpometacarpal joint, between the trapezium (a carpal bone) and the first metacarpal bone at the base of the thumb
thumb can move within the same plane as the palm of the hand, or it can jut out anteriorly, perpendicular to the palm = opposable thumb

Saddle joint. Adapted from: Produnis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Thumb joints. Credit: LittleT889, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Saddle Joint: At a saddle joint, both of the articulating surfaces for the bones have a saddle shape, which is concave in one direction and convex in the other. This allows the two bones to fit together like a rider sitting on a saddle. 

Saddle joints are functionally classified as biaxial joints. The primary example is the first carpometacarpal joint, between the trapezium (a carpal bone) and the first metacarpal bone at the base of the thumb. This joint provides the thumb the ability for angular movement away from the palm of the hand along two planes. Thus, the thumb can move within the same plane as the palm of the hand, or it can jut out anteriorly, perpendicular to the palm. This movement of the first carpometacarpal joint is what gives humans their distinctive “opposable” thumbs.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Plane joint (gliding joint)
flat or slightly curved articulating surfaces 
allows for gliding movement where bones slide back and forth against each other
motion is small and tightly constrained by surrounding ligaments
technically multiaxial, but ligaments constrain some directions of movement
functionally thus exhibit only one or few movements
e.g., intercarpal joints (between carpal bones) of wrist
e.g., intertarsal joints (between tarsal bones) of foot
e.g., zygapophysial joints (between superior and inferior articular processes of adjacent vertebrae)

Types of Synovial Joints. The six types of synovial joints allow the body to move in a variety of ways. (d) Plane joints, such as those between the tarsal bones of the foot, allow for limited gliding movements between bones.

Zygapophysial (facet) joints. Credit: Dr.foksha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Plane Joint: At a plane joint (also called a gliding joint), the articulating surfaces of the bones are flat or slightly curved and of approximately the same size, which allows for predominantly gliding movement where the bones slide back and forth against each other. The motion at this type of joint is usually small and tightly constrained by surrounding ligaments. It is worth noting that based only on their shape, plane joints have the ability to allow multiple movements, including rotation. Thus, plane joints can be functionally classified as a multiaxial joint. However, not all of these movements are available to every plane joint due to limitations placed on it by ligaments or neighboring bones. Thus, depending upon the specific joint of the body, a plane joint may exhibit only a single type of movement or several movements. 

Plane joints are found between the carpal bones (intercarpal joints) of the wrist or tarsal bones (intertarsal joints) of the foot, or between the superior and inferior articular processes of adjacent vertebrae (zygapophysial joints).

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Ball-and-socket joint
joint with the greatest range of motion
rounded head of one bone (ball) fits into concave articulation (socket) of adjacent bone 
only 2 in body:
hip joint
femur articulates with hip bone
shoulder (glenohumeral) joint
humerus articulates with glenoid cavity of the scapula

Types of Synovial Joints. The six types of synovial joints allow the body to move in a variety of ways. (f) The hip and shoulder joints are the only ball-and-socket joints of the body.

Ball-and-socket joint. Adapted from: Produnis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Ball-and-Socket Joint: The joint with the greatest range of motion is the ball-and-socket joint. At these joints, the rounded head of one bone (the ball) fits into the concave articulation (the socket) of the adjacent bone. 

The hip joint and the glenohumeral (or shoulder) joint are the only ball-and-socket joints of the body. At the hip joint, the head of the femur articulates with the acetabulum of the hip bone, and at the shoulder joint, the head of the humerus articulates with the glenoid cavity of the scapula.

slides.title: Part 4: Synovial Joints
slides.body:
Part 4: Synovial Joints

Ball-and-socket joint
multiaxial
rotate around their long axis (rotation)
medial-lateral (adduction-abduction)
anterior-posterior (flexion-extension)
circumduction – the distal end of the bone moves in a circle while the proximal end remains relatively stationary (flexion -> abduction -> extension -> adduction)

Shoulder motions. Credit: Modified from Z-Anatomy (CC-BY-SA 4.0) by D. Rittenhouse.

Movements of the body.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Ball-and-socket joints are classified functionally as multiaxial joints. The femur and the humerus are able to effect angular movements in both anterior-posterior (flexion-extension) and medial-lateral (adduction-abduction) directions and they can also rotate (rotation) around their long axis. 

Please note that while flexion is usually an anterior movement, including of the upper limbs, wrist, and fingers while standing in anatomical position, in the lower leg, flexion involves a posterior movement. Hence, for limbs, it is easiest to remember that flexion involves the reduction of angle between bones, while extension involves the opposite.

These multiaxial ball-and-socket joints also allow for a complex movement called circumduction. In this instance, the distal end of the bone moves in a circle while the proximal end remains relatively stationary. Circumduction of the arm and leg are possible at ball-and-socket joints.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Okay. We now move on to the final section of this unit, Part 5: Movements of the body. We’ve already covered some of these movements during our discussion of synovial joints, but we will present them again, in a systematic manner, here.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Movements determined by muscles on either side of an articulation (a joint)
one muscle contracts
other muscle relaxes
Type of movement determined by 4 factors:
orientation of the muscle
between origin and insertion points
action of other muscles
jointly attached to origin or insertion bones
type of joint between the bones
muscle tension
limiting excess movement (e.g., hamstrings when touching toes)

Movements of the Joints

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Synovial joints allow the body a tremendous range of movements. Each movement at a synovial joint results from the contraction or relaxation of the muscles that are attached to the bones on either side of the articulation. 

The type of movement that can be produced at a synovial joint is determined by four factors:
1. The orientation of the muscle between its origin and an insertion point. 
2. The actions of other muscles that may insert and/or originate on the same bones.
3. The type of joint between the bones. 
4. Muscle tension. This is a limitation that works in a similar manner to tension in the ligaments. An example of the role of muscle tension is demonstrated when touching one’s toes with the knees straight. The movement is restricted by the tension of the hamstring muscles.

There are many types of movement that can occur at synovial joints. Movement types are generally paired, with one being the opposite of the other. Body movements are always described in relation to the anatomical position of the body: upright stance, with upper limbs to the side of body and palms facing forward.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Flexion and extension (vertebral column)
involves both symphysis joints (cartilaginous) and plane joints (synovial)
anterior/posterior movements within sagittal plane
flexion (or anterior flexion) is an anterior-directed
extension is posterior-directed
lateral flexion – toward side

Movements of the Body, Part 1.

Intervertebral Disc.

Plane joint.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Flexion and Extension
Flexion and extension are movements that take place within the sagittal plane and involve anterior or posterior movements of the body or limbs. 

For the vertebral column, flexion (or anterior flexion) is an anterior bending of the neck or body, while extension involves a posterior-directed motion, such as straightening from a flexed position or bending backward. Lateral flexion is the bending of the neck or body toward the right or left side. 

These movements of the vertebral column involve both the symphysis joint formed by each intervertebral disc, as well as the plane type of synovial joint formed between the inferior articular processes of one vertebra and the superior articular processes of the next lower vertebra.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Flexion and extension (limbs)
involves hinge, condyloid, saddle, and ball-and-socket joints
flexion decreases angle between bones (bends joint)
extension increases angle (straightens joint)
for upper limbs:
flexion is anterior-directed
for thumb: extension is thumb away from palm, within the same plane as the palm, flexion brings it back against index finger or into palm
for lower limb:
flexion in thigh is anterior-directed
flexion in leg and foot is posterior-directed (knee flexion)

Movements of the Body, Part 1.

Types of Synovial Joints

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In the limbs, flexion decreases the angle between the bones (that is, it bends the joint), while extension increases the angle and straightens the joint.

For the upper limbs, all anterior-going motions are flexion and all posterior-going motions are extension. These include anterior-posterior movements of the arm at the shoulder, the forearm at the elbow, the hand at the wrist, and the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints. For the thumb, extension moves the thumb away from the palm of the hand, within the same plane as the palm, while flexion brings the thumb back against the index finger or into the palm. These motions take place at the first carpometacarpal joint. 

In the lower limbs, bringing the thigh forward and upward is flexion at the hip joint, while any posterior-going motion of the thigh is extension. Knee flexion is the bending of the knee to bring the foot toward the posterior thigh, and extension is the straightening of the knee. 

Flexion and extension movements are seen at the hinge, condyloid, saddle, and ball-and-socket joints of the limbs.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Hyperextension
excessive extension of a joint beyond its normal range of motion, thus resulting in injury
Hyperflexion
excessive flexion at a joint, which can also cause injury

Movements of the Body, Part 1.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Hyperextension

Hyperextension is the abnormal or excessive extension of a joint beyond its normal range of motion, thus resulting in injury. 

Similarly, hyperflexion is excessive flexion at a joint. 

Hyperextension injuries are common at hinge joints such as the knee or elbow. In cases of “whiplash” in which the head is suddenly moved backward and then forward, a patient may experience both hyperextension and hyperflexion of the cervical region.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Abduction and adduction
involve condyloid, saddle, and ball-and-socket joints
medial-lateral movements within coronal plane
abduction – moves limb laterally
adduction – moves limb medially
For limbs and wrist
abduction moves away from body
For fingers or toes
spreading of fingers or toes is abduction

Movements of the Body, Part 1.

Types of Synovial Joints

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Abduction and Adduction
Abduction and adduction motions occur within the coronal plane and involve medial-lateral motions of the limbs, fingers, toes, or thumb. Abduction moves the limb laterally away from the midline of the body, while adduction is the opposing movement that brings the limb toward the body or across the midline. For example, abduction is raising the arm at the shoulder joint, moving it laterally away from the body, while adduction brings the arm down to the side of the body. Similarly, abduction and adduction at the wrist moves the hand away from or toward the midline of the body. Because the thumb is oriented almost perpendicular to the other fingers, abduction of the thumb means moving it anteriorly away from the palm, while adduction returns it in line with the other fingers.

Spreading the fingers or toes, apart is also abduction, while bringing the fingers or toes together is adduction. 

Abduction and adduction movements are seen at condyloid, saddle, and ball-and-socket joints.

slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Opposition and reposition
opposable thumb allows for grasping and varied tool use in primates
opposition of thumb brings the thumb tip into contact with the tip of the fingers of same hand
reposition brings the thumb back next to the index finger
involves abduction/adduction and flexion/extension…

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Shoulder motions. Credit: Modified from Z-Anatomy (CC-BY-SA 4.0) by D. Rittenhouse.
slides.notes:
Opposition and Reposition

Opposition of the thumb brings the tip of the thumb into contact with the tip of the fingers of the same hand and reposition brings the thumb back next to the index finger. 

The evolution of the opposable thumb allows for grasping and varied tool use in primates.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Circumduction
involves condyloid and saddle joints (which are biaxial) and ball-and-sockets joints (which are multiaxial)
movement of a body region in a circular manner
one end stays relatively stationary
other end moves in a circle. 
involves the sequential combination of flexion, adduction, extension, and abduction at a joint

Movements of the Body, Part 1.

Types of Synovial Joints

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Circumduction
Circumduction is the movement of a body region in a circular manner, in which one end of the body region being moved stays relatively stationary while the other end describes a circle. It involves the sequential combination of flexion, adduction, extension, and abduction at a joint. 

This type of motion is found at biaxial condyloid and saddle joints, and at multiaxial ball-and-sockets joints.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Rotation
involves pivot joint, or a ball-and-socket joint within vertebral column
produced by the summation of the small rotational movements available between adjacent vertebrae

Movements of the Body, Part 1.

Types of Synovial Joints

Shoulder motions. Credit: Modified from Z-Anatomy (CC-BY-SA 4.0) by D. Rittenhouse.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Rotation
Rotation can occur within the vertebral column, at a pivot joint, or at a ball-and-socket joint. 

Rotation of the neck or body is the twisting movement produced by the summation of the small rotational movements available between adjacent vertebrae. At a pivot joint, one bone rotates in relation to another bone. This is a uniaxial joint, and thus rotation is the only motion allowed at a pivot joint. For example, at the atlantoaxial joint, the first cervical vertebra (the atlas) rotates around the dens, the upward projection from the second cervical vertebra (the axis). This allows the head to rotate from side to side as when shaking the head “no.” 

Rotation can also occur at the ball-and-socket joints of the shoulder and hip. Here, the humerus and femur rotate around their long axis, which moves the anterior surface of the arm or thigh either toward or away from the midline of the body. Movement that brings the anterior surface of the limb toward the midline of the body is called medial (or internal) rotation. Conversely, rotation of the limb so that the anterior surface moves away from the midline is lateral (or external) rotation. 

Be sure to distinguish medial and lateral rotation, which can only occur at the multiaxial shoulder and hip joints, from circumduction, which can occur at either biaxial or multiaxial joints.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Supination and pronation
supination and pronation are movements involving rotation
proximal radioulnar joint is a pivot joint formed by the head of the radius and its articulation with the ulna 
supinated position
palms are supinated in anatomical position
radius and ulna are parallel
pronated position
radius and ulna are crossed

Movements of the Body, Part 2.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Arm movements. Credit: Modified from Z-Anatomy (CC-BY-SA 4.0) by D. Rittenhouse.
slides.notes:
Supination and Pronation

The proximal radioulnar joint is a pivot joint formed by the head of the radius and its articulation with the ulna. This joint allows for the radius to rotate along its length during pronation and supination movements of the forearm. 

In the anatomical position, the upper limb is held next to the body with the palm facing forward. This is the supinated position of the forearm. In this position, the radius and ulna are parallel to each other. You can remember this position easily, as your would hold a bowl of soup on your palm in the supinated position… the bowl would fall out of your palm in the pronated position. The pronated position has the palm of the hand facing backward, and the radius and ulna form an X-shape.

Supination and pronation are the movements of the forearm that go between the supinated and pronated positions.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion
movements at the “ankle joint proper” (hinge joint between tibia, fibula, and talus bone)
dorsiflexion – lifting top of foot
plantar flexion – lifting heel / pointing toes downward

Movements of the Body, Part 2.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Dorsiflexion and Plantar Flexion

Dorsiflexion and plantar flexion are movements at the ankle joint, which is a hinge joint. Lifting the front of the foot, so that the top of the foot moves toward the anterior leg is dorsiflexion, while lifting the heel of the foot from the ground or pointing the toes downward is plantar flexion. These are the only movements available at the ankle joint.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Inversion and eversion
involve multiple plane joints among tarsal bones (at intertarsal joints)
inversion – turning of the foot to angle the bottom of the foot toward the midline
eversion – turning of the foot to angle the bottom of the foot away from the midline

Movements of the Body, Part 2.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Inversion and Eversion

Inversion and eversion are complex movements that involve the multiple plane joints among the tarsal bones of the posterior foot (thus at intertarsal joints, and not the ankle joint). 

Inversion is the turning of the foot to angle the bottom of the foot toward the midline, while eversion turns the bottom of the foot away from the midline. These are important motions that help to stabilize the foot when walking or running on an uneven surface and aid in the quick side-to-side changes in direction used during active sports such as basketball or soccer.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Depression and elevation
downward or upward movements of the scapula or mandible
elevation 
scapula – upward movement of the scapula and shoulder 
mandible – upward movement of lower jaw to close mouth or bite
depression 
scapula – downward movement of the scapula and shoulder 
mandible – downward movement of lower jaw to open mouth

Movements of the Body, Part 2.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Depression and Elevation

Depression and elevation are downward and upward movements of the scapula or mandible. The upward movement of the scapula and shoulder is elevation, while a downward movement is depression. These movements are used to shrug your shoulders. Similarly, elevation of the mandible is the upward movement of the lower jaw used to close the mouth or bite on something, and depression is the downward movement that produces opening of the mouth.

slides.title: Part 5: Movements of the body
slides.body:
Part 5: Movements of the body

Protraction and retraction
anterior-posterior movements of the scapula or mandible
protraction 
scapula – shoulder is moved forward and laterally, as when pushing against something or throwing a ball
mandible – pushing chin out (also called protrusion since only forward, not lateral)
retraction 
scapula – scapula pulled posteriorly and medially, toward the vertebral column
mandible – pulling lower jaw backward (also called retrusion)
mandible can also move side-to-side (excursion)
multiple movements possible due to presence of both a hinge and plane joint

Movements of the Body, Part 2.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Protraction and Retraction

Protraction and retraction are anterior-posterior movements of the scapula or mandible. Protraction of the scapula occurs when the shoulder is moved forward and laterally, as when pushing against something or throwing a ball. Retraction is the opposite motion, with the scapula being pulled posteriorly and medially, toward the vertebral column. 

For the mandible, protraction occurs when the lower jaw is pushed forward, to stick out the chin, while retraction pulls the lower jaw backward.
